title: California Sales Tax: Rates, Taxability, & Compliance Guide
summary: California sales tax ranges from 7.25% to 11.75%. See rates by city, how district taxes work, what’s taxable (including SaaS in 2027), and resale rules.
body_markdown:
## California sales tax at a glance


**State taxing authority** California Department of Tax and Fee Administration


**State sales tax rate** 6%


**Local tax rates** 1.25% mandatory local tax, district taxes ranging from 0% to 4.5%


**Combined sales tax rate range** 7.25% to 11.75%


**Economic nexus threshold** Over $500,000 in combined sales of tangible personal property delivered into California during the current or previous calendar year


**Website**[cdtfa.ca.gov](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/)


**Tax phone line** 1-800-400-7115


California’s sales tax structure is unique because it consists of a state base rate, mandatory local taxes, and optional district taxes that vary by city, county, or special voting district. This means total combined sales and use tax rates range from 7.25% to 11.75%.


California also has one of the highest economic nexus thresholds in the country at $500,000 in combined sales of tangible personal property. Most tangible personal property is subject to sales tax, with notable exceptions for groceries, prescription drugs, and certain medical devices.


SaaS and other prewritten software were exempt but become taxable on Jan. 1, 2027. Most other digital products remain tax-exempt.


California businesses with sales tax nexus must register with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) and must file and remit taxes online or by mail.


## California sales tax rates and calculations


For taxable transactions in California, combined sales and use tax rates range from 7.25% to 11.75%. These rates include the state tax rate, mandatory local taxes, and variable district taxes.


California’s statewide base rate is 7.25%. It includes the 6% state rate, the[1% Bradley-Burns local tax](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/industry/local-jurisdictions-and-districts/getting-started.htm) , which goes to the city or county where the sale occurs, and a 0.25% Local Transportation Fund tax, which goes to the county where the sale occurs. These amounts apply statewide.


Cities, counties, and other local districts can also add district taxes, usually approved by voters for specific purposes such as infrastructure or public services. Some districts have no additional tax. A district’s tax can be either a sales tax or a use tax.


California has two related taxes on tangible goods. Retailers located in California collect sales tax on their sales. Out-of-state retailers with[nexus in California](https://www.numeral.com/nexus/california) collect use tax on taxable sales delivered into California. A remote seller has nexus once its California sales exceed $500,000 in the current or preceding calendar year.

### How to calculate California sales tax


To calculate California sales tax, start with the base rate of 7.25%, which includes both state and local taxes. Then, add the district taxes in your location, which can be up to 4.5%. Then, apply that percentage rate to the item's sale price.


Say you’re selling a $50 item in Los Angeles, which has a 3% district tax rate and a 10.25% combined tax rate. Your sales tax calculation would look like this:


$50 x .1025 = $5.13


Then add the sales tax to the item price to get the total cost. In this situation, the total price would be $55.13.


### Origin vs. destination sourcing in California


California uses different sourcing practices for local taxes and district taxes.


Local sales taxes for shipped items are generally allocated to the retailer’s place of business where the sale occurs. Businesses remit these taxes to CDTFA, which distributes them to the appropriate local governments.


Different allocation rules apply to local use taxes collected by out-of-state retailers. These allocation rules don’t affect the local tax rate, which is the same statewide.


District taxes on shipped items generally depend on where the buyer receives the product. Sellers must collect the applicable district use tax when they are engaged in business in the destination district.


Retailers whose combined sales of tangible personal property delivered into California exceed $500,000 in the current or previous calendar year generally must collect applicable district taxes statewide.


For example, if a company based in San Francisco ships a taxable product to a customer in San Diego and is required to collect San Diego’s district tax, it would collect the combined rate of 7.75% instead of San Francisco’s 8.625%.


### Is California a Streamlined Sales Tax (SST) state?


No, California is not a Streamlined Sales Tax state. Out-of-state retailers with sales tax nexus in California must register, file, and remit taxes directly through the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration instead of using the Streamlined Sales Tax system.


## Sales tax nexus in California


Nexus is the legal connection between a business and a state that requires it to register, collect, and remit sales tax in that state.


Three different types of sales tax nexus are important in California:


- **Physical:** A business has a physical presence in the state, such as a store or office. See Numeral’s[physical nexus guide](https://www.numeral.com/blog/physical-nexus) .
- **Economic:** The business conducts a certain amount of economic activity in the state. See Numeral’s[economic nexus guide](https://www.numeral.com/blog/economic-nexus) .
- **Marketplace:** The business sells to customers in the state through a digital marketplace. See Numeral’s[marketplace facilitator guide](https://www.numeral.com/blog/marketplace-facilitator) .


Here are the specific requirements for[California sales tax nexus](https://www.numeral.com/nexus/california) :


Nexus type Requirements


Physical A business has physical nexus if it has a business office, retail store, warehouse, or other property; has employees or contractors; or has inventory in a third-party warehouse in California.


Economic Businesses have economic nexus if they have combined sales of[over $500,000 in tangible personal property](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/industry/wayfair/) delivered into CA in the current or previous calendar year.


Marketplace Marketplace providers are responsible for collecting and remitting California sales tax on behalf of their sellers. However, a seller’s marketplace sales count toward their economic nexus, even if they don’t pay the taxes themselves.


Both taxable and nontaxable sales of tangible personal property count toward the threshold, including sales made through marketplace facilitators.


California also has[trailing nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/trailing-nexus) . This means that if a business had sales tax nexus in California during a calendar year, they must continue filing and remitting sales tax in California through the entire following calendar year, even if they no longer meet the nexus threshold.


## What’s taxable and exempt in California


Most tangible personal property is subject to sales tax in California, but there are some exceptions. Here’s an overview of taxability for key product categories.


Category Generally taxable? Notes


Tangible personal property Yes


Groceries No Most grocery items and cold prepared foods are tax-exempt, while hot prepared foods, soft drinks, and alcoholic beverages are taxable.


Clothing Yes


Prescription drugs No Prescription drugs and most medical devices are tax-exempt.


SaaS No (as of 2026) SaaS will become taxable in California in 2027.


Digital goods No (as of 2026) Prewritten software, including software accessed remotely, becomes taxable Jan. 1, 2027; most other digital products stay exempt.


Services No Most services are tax-exempt, unless the services are used to create new tangible personal property.


Shipping Varies Separately stated shipping charges are generally exempt up to the actual delivery cost when goods are shipped by a common carrier, independent contract carrier, or USPS. Excess charges and handling fees are generally taxable on taxable sales.


### What’s subject to sales tax in California?


Many items are[subject to sales tax in California](https://taxes.ca.gov/sales-and-use-tax/whats-taxable/) , including:


- Most tangible personal property, including clothing
- Hot food, soft drinks, alcoholic beverages, and food supplements
- Services involved in the creation of new tangible personal property


### What’s exempt from sales tax in California?


California has several notable sales tax exemptions, including:


- Groceries
- Prescription drugs
- Certain medical devices
- Most services
- Shipping charges in some situations


### SaaS and digital goods taxability in California


California’s sales tax applies to tangible personal property, so[SaaS](https://www.numeral.com/blog/saas-sales-tax-california) and most digital products have not been taxable in the past.


However,[California SB 122](https://www.numeral.com/blog/california-sb-122) changes that. The[legislation](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billCompareClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB122&showamends=false) requires that, starting Jan. 1, 2027, prewritten software is taxable, whether it is downloaded, accessed remotely, or licensed. SaaS, or subscription access to software, is also taxable.


Most other digital products stay exempt, including digital books, digital audio and audiovisual works such as streaming video and podcasts, digital video games, digital artwork, digital assets such as cryptocurrency, and digital infrastructure. Custom software built to a single customer’s order is also exempt.


### Resale and exemption certificates in California


[California’s Resale Certificate](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/formspubs/cdtfa230.pdf) allows businesses to make tax-free purchases if the items are intended for resale.


When filling out this form, businesses must provide information about their business and the items they plan to purchase for resale. They must include their California seller’s permit number or explain why they aren’t required to hold one.


Businesses can give each vendor a blanket resale certificate covering multiple purchases and product types, as long as the certificate adequately describes the items.


A California[resale certificate](https://www.numeral.com/blog/resale-certificates) remains in effect until the buyer revokes it in writing. A buyer who must hold a California seller’s permit must list a valid permit number on the certificate. A buyer who doesn’t need a permit must explain why on the certificate instead.


After filling out the Resale Certificate, businesses should submit it to the vendor when they are making a purchase. Resale certificates do not need to be submitted directly to the California government. Both buyers and sellers should keep copies of resale certificates for at least four years in case of a future tax audit.


Businesses using[out-of-state resale certificates](https://www.numeral.com/blog/states-that-dont-accept-out-of-state-resale-certificates) must ensure the documentation meets California’s requirements.


CDTFA does not require a specific form: A[Multistate Tax Commission](https://www.mtc.gov/resources/uniform-sales-use-tax-exemption-certificate/) certificate or another document can qualify if it includes all required information, including a California seller’s permit number when required or an explanation of why the buyer does not need one.


## Registering for a California seller’s permit


To[register for a California seller’s permit](https://www.numeral.com/sales-tax-registration/california) , apply through[CDTFA’s online portal](https://onlineservices.cdtfa.ca.gov/_/) . If you plan to make sales for less than 90 days, you can register for a temporary seller’s permit instead.


During the application process, you’ll need to provide[information about yourself and your business](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/services/registration.htm) . You’ll also need to create a username and password, set up a security question, and enable two-factor authentication.


Select “Register a New Business Activity,” then select “Seller’s Permit.” From there, you’ll need to provide the following information:


- Employer Identification Number
- California Secretary of State identification number
- Registered DBA name, if applicable
- NAICS/SIC business activity codes
- Owner’s SSN and date of birth
- Owner’s ID number
- Owner’s contact information
- Business address
- Business sales information
- Contact information for bookkeepers and suppliers


Most businesses receive their seller’s permit immediately after completing the application. However, some applications may require manual review, which can take a few days.


Once you receive your seller’s permit, save your account number for future returns. California seller’s permits do not expire as long as your business is active and continues to file and remit sales tax.


California does not charge an application fee for seller’s permits. However, some businesses may be required to pay a[security deposit](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/taxes-and-fees/faqseller.htm) to cover any unpaid taxes. The deposit amount can range anywhere from[$2,000 to $50,000](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/taxes-and-fees/manuals/cpm-04.pdf) , depending on your estimated sales volume.


Although many California cities and counties levy local district taxes, you don’t need to set up separate local sales tax accounts. The California Department of Tax and Fee Administration collects all sales taxes and distributes them to the appropriate local government agencies.


### Registration requirements for remote sellers


If your business is based in another state, you’ll need to[register](https://www.numeral.com/product/registrations) with the CDTFA once you exceed California’s economic nexus threshold or establish physical nexus in the state.


A remote seller must generally register if its combined sales of tangible personal property delivered into California exceed $500,000 in the current or previous calendar year. An exception generally applies if all California sales are made through registered marketplace facilitators responsible for collecting the tax.


If your business isn’t required to register, you can still[voluntarily apply](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/industry/out-of-state-retailers/registration.htm) for a Certificate of Registration – Use Tax and collect and remit use tax for your California customers.


Out-of-state sellers can apply through CDTFA’s online registration system. The information required depends on the business’s structure and California activities.


## Collecting California sales tax


Once you’ve registered for your seller’s permit, the next step is to start collecting sales tax on every taxable transaction in California.


Use the following steps to collect sales tax for each transaction:


1. Determine whether the product is taxable or exempt.
2. Determine the sourcing location for district taxes. For online orders, this is usually based on the buyer’s shipping address.
3. Apply the correct state, local, and district tax rate to the sale.
4. Collect the tax from the customer as part of the transaction.
5. Track collected tax for future filing and reporting.


Most ecommerce platforms and point-of-sale systems now have features that will automatically calculate and apply the correct sales tax rate based on your location and the buyer’s location. This means you do not have to manually calculate and collect sales tax for every transaction.


### Marketplace sales


In California, websites like Amazon and Etsy are considered “[marketplace facilitators](https://www.numeral.com/blog/marketplace-facilitator) .” These companies are required to collect, file, and remit sales taxes on behalf of their sellers. If you sell products in California exclusively through a marketplace platform, you are not responsible for filing and remitting sales tax yourself.


However, if you make both direct sales and marketplace sales, you’ll need to track your marketplace activity. Marketplace sales count towards California’s economic nexus threshold of $500,000, even though you are not remitting the taxes yourself.


If you are a marketplace seller with sales tax nexus and you have an active seller’s permit, you’ll also need to report your marketplace activity on your sales tax returns. However, the marketplace facilitator still collects and remits the taxes for these sales.


### Shipping and delivery charges


[Shipping and delivery charges](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-on-shipping) are exempt from sales tax in California if they meet the following criteria:


- Goods are shipped via USPS, a common carrier like UPS or FedEx, or an independent contract carrier.
- The shipping charge is listed as a separate line item on the invoice.
- The exempt portion of the shipping charge does not exceed the actual cost of the delivery.


You must keep records of the shipping costs to prove that they are tax-exempt.


If a separately stated shipping charge exceeds the actual qualifying delivery cost, the excess is generally taxable. Handling charges are also generally taxable when the items sold are taxable. Other delivery arrangements may be taxable depending on the circumstances.


## Filing and paying California sales tax


After registering for a seller’s permit, the CDTFA will assign you a filing frequency. Filing frequencies are based on the business’s sales volume.


Most businesses need to[file and remit](https://www.numeral.com/product/filing-and-remittance) sales taxes quarterly. However, some businesses are required to file sales taxes monthly or annually instead.


Sales tax returns must be filed by the[last day of the month](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/taxes-and-fees/sales-use-tax-returns-filing-dates.htm) following the reporting period. For example, first-quarter taxes are due on April 30. If this date falls on a weekend or state holiday, the due date is extended to the next business day.


Businesses with nexus are always required to file a return, even if they have zero sales to report.


Some businesses may also be required to follow a monthly prepayment schedule, even when filing quarterly. Prepayments are generally due on the 24th of the second and third months of each quarter.


For example, January’s prepayment is due Feb. 24, and February’s is due March 24. A special rule applies to the second quarter: The June 24 prepayment covers May 1 through June 15. If a deadline falls on a weekend or state holiday, it moves to the next business day.


The most efficient way to file and remit California sales tax is through the CDTFA’s online portal. However, you can also file and remit by mail using a check or money order. You’ll need to include your account number, and all returns must be postmarked on or before the due date.


### Filing California sales tax online


You can file California sales tax online through the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration.


You can use this system to remit state, local, and district sales taxes on the same return. You can make payments online using an ACH bank transfer, credit card, or debit card. Credit and debit transactions may be subject to processing fees.


Numeral’s[step-by-step guide](https://www.numeral.com/blog/how-to-file-california-sales-tax-online) for California walks through the process screen by screen.


## California sales tax penalties and interest


If you file and remit your California sales taxes late, you could be charged[penalties and interest](https://www.numeral.com/blog/what-happens-if-you-dont-collect-or-remit-sales-tax) .


California charges a 10% late-filing fee and a 10% late-payment fee. However, these penalties do not stack, so if you both file and pay your taxes late, the fee will not exceed 10% of the tax due.


If you are required to make sales tax prepayments and miss a prepayment deadline, you may pay a fee of 6% to 10%, depending on the circumstances.


California also charges interest on late sales tax payments. The interest rate is currently 10% per year, or 0.83% per month. Interest continues to accrue until the payment is made in full.


## California sales tax recordkeeping and audits


Businesses in California should keep detailed records of their sales and tax filings. These include:


- California sales tax returns
- Receipts, invoices, or bills
- Bookkeeping ledgers
- Resale exemption certificates
- Purchase records


The CDTFA can[audit](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-audit) your sales tax returns to make sure you accurately reported your sales and remitted the correct amount of tax.


Audits usually cover three years, but can extend up to eight years in some circumstances. California businesses should keep their sales tax records for at least this long to ensure they’re prepared for an audit.


If you are subject to an audit and disagree with the results, you can protest it by filing a Petition for Redetermination and attending an appeals conference. If this does not resolve the issue, you can appeal to California’s[Office of Tax Appeals](https://ota.ca.gov/) .

## California sales tax FAQs


**What is the sales tax rate in California?**
California’s combined sales tax rate ranges from 7.25% to 11.75%. This includes 6% state tax, 1.25% required local tax, and variable district taxes.


**What is the economic nexus threshold in California?**
The economic nexus threshold in California is over $500,000 in combined sales of tangible personal property during the current or previous calendar year.


**Is SaaS taxable in California?**
SaaS and other prewritten software become taxable on Jan. 1, 2027. Most other digital products remain exempt.


**Do I need a sales tax permit in California?**
Businesses with sales tax nexus in California generally must register with CDTFA for a seller’s permit or a Certificate of Registration – Use Tax, depending on their activities. Registration generally isn’t required if all California sales are made through registered marketplace facilitators that collect and remit the tax.
